title: Claude wrote an InDesign script that eliminated monthly manual PDF work
whatTried: Used Claude to write a script for Adobe InDesign to mass-rename and correctly output PDF files — a task that had previously required significant manual effort each month.
whatSurprisedMe: The script worked. Claude generated functional InDesign automation code without needing to know how to write scripts.
whatWorked: Giving Claude the specific task (rename and output PDFs in a certain format) and letting it write the automation. The output was production-ready.

title: Flat plan automation worked technically — but brand diversity made it useless
whatTried: Attempted to automate flat plans in Adobe InDesign using AI.
whatSurprisedMe: The tool worked technically, but the diversity of brand requirements across SJC titles meant the automated output wasn't actually usable in practice.
whatFailed: The output didn't account for how different each brand's requirements were. The diversity wasn't something that could be templated away.
nextTime: Prioritize solving problems that already exist and have been explicitly stated. Avoid building automation for anticipated problems that may not actually exist.

title: ClickUp AI runs editorial calendars, trending topics, weekly reports, and invoices
whatTried: Used ClickUp AI agents to manage editorial calendars, identify trending social media topics, automate weekly reporting with percentage changes, and handle invoice generation.
whatSurprisedMe: The AI agents can update their own instructions based on user feedback — the workflow actually improves as you use it.
whatWorked: All four use cases ran well inside ClickUp. Having everything in one platform kept the workflow tight.

title: Uploaded raw screen captures to Claude and got a full performance report in minutes
whatTried: Uploaded raw screen captures and data from influencer PR box campaigns to Claude to reorganize presentation decks and generate performance reports.
whatSurprisedMe: A report that would have taken days was produced in minutes from raw, unstructured visual inputs.
whatWorked: Feeding Claude raw screen captures rather than cleaned data. Claude interpreted the visual context and structured the analysis without needing formatted inputs.

title: Claude read Webflow screenshots and gave working code — no dev background needed
whatTried: Uploaded screenshots of the desired layout and the Webflow interface to Claude to get help implementing features like embedded videos.
whatSurprisedMe: Received step-by-step instructions and functional code without any prior development knowledge.
whatWorked: Using screenshots as the input rather than trying to describe the problem in text. Visual context was enough for Claude to understand exactly what was needed.

title: Gemini Gems follow custom instructions too literally — wording precision matters
whatTried: Created Gems (Gemini custom AI assistants with custom instructions) to handle repeatable workflows.
whatSurprisedMe: The AI followed instructions too literally, producing unexpected behaviour that required multiple rounds of revision.
whatWorked: The concept of Gems — a persistent, customised assistant for a specific workflow — is genuinely useful.
whatFailed: Instruction wording needs to be precise. Ambiguity in custom instructions leads to the AI applying them in ways you didn't intend.
nextTime: Treat the first version of custom instructions as a draft and refine based on how the AI actually interprets them.

title: Pasted a 5-page Google Doc into ClickUp — it auto-mapped everything into task fields
whatTried: Copied and pasted a four-to-five-page Google Doc directly into ClickUp AI.
whatSurprisedMe: The AI automatically mapped the content into pre-existing ClickUp fields, creating a structured single source of truth from an unstructured document.
whatWorked: The copy-paste approach was simpler than expected. No formatting or cleanup needed before ingesting.

title: ChatGPT generates AB test variants and checks editorial against client briefs
whatTried: Used ChatGPT to generate multiple variations of ad creative for AB testing and to verify that editorial concepts and articles align with client creative briefs.
whatSurprisedMe: The time savings were significant even though every output still needed human editing before it was final.
whatWorked: Generating many variants quickly and selecting the best ones — rather than crafting a single version manually — consistently produced better candidates.
whatFailed: Output is rarely final. Human editing is always required before anything goes to a client.

title: Lovable and Emergent AI rapid-prototype branded content sites — but credit limits hit fast
whatTried: Tested Lovable and Emergent AI for creating website designs for branded content projects.
whatSurprisedMe: Both tools were useful for rapid prototyping — far faster than building manually.
whatWorked: Getting to a visual prototype quickly without developer involvement.
whatFailed: Hit credit limits during testing, which interrupted the workflow before a full evaluation was complete.

title: Google AI Studio generates pitches from pure prompts — no subscription needed
whatTried: Used Google AI Studio with pure prompts (no pre-built tools or integrations) to generate pitches quickly.
whatSurprisedMe: It produced usable pitch content as a cost-effective alternative to paid tools — viable for early-stage testing without committing to a subscription.
whatWorked: Direct prompting in AI Studio for early-stage ideation and pitch generation.

title: Claude built a working editor navigation prototype — weeks of dev work in a session
whatTried: Used Claude (alongside Gemini and ChatGPT as thought partners) to create a functional prototype for editor navigation to test a product idea.
whatSurprisedMe: The prototype worked well enough to validate the concept immediately, compressing the time between idea and tangible output significantly.
whatWorked: Using Claude as more than a writing tool — as an active builder and technical thought partner for product ideas.

title: Gemini finds experts by writing voice and publication history — with contact info
whatTried: Used Gemini to find experts matching specific parameters: a lively writing voice, a particular publication history, and specific subject matter expertise.
whatSurprisedMe: Gemini returned expert matches with contact information and relevant links — not just names. It interpreted qualitative criteria like writing voice effectively.
whatWorked: Specifying writing style and voice as a search parameter, not just subject expertise.

title: ChatGPT for brainstorming, Claude for modeling — matching the tool to the thinking type
whatTried: Used ChatGPT as a sounding board and brainstorming partner, and Claude for modeling work. Also combined Excel workbooks with AI for complex financial models and year-over-year trend reporting.
whatSurprisedMe: The two tools have meaningfully different strengths for cognitive tasks. Claude handles structured analysis better; ChatGPT is more generative and conversational.
whatWorked: Matching the tool to the task type rather than defaulting to one tool for everything. Excel + AI for trend analysis replaced work that previously needed dedicated analyst support.

title: AI handles multi-year sales analysis, benchmark reporting, pitch imagery, and prospecting lists
whatTried: Used AI to analyze sales categories (print, digital, events) across multiple years, summarize campaign performance against benchmarks, adjust tone of difficult negotiation communications, generate visual ideas for event sponsorship decks, and build prospecting lists for brands advertising around specific periods.
whatSurprisedMe: Tasks that were previously manual and time-consuming — trend comparisons, benchmark summaries, prospecting lists, searching for images — became fast enough to do on demand.
whatWorked: Applying AI across the full sales workflow rather than just one task. Each use case compounded the time savings.

title: ClickUp Super Agent builds a searchable study bank from PR pitches — surfaced automatically at story time
whatTried: Used a ClickUp Super Agent to create a list for tracking studies received from PR reps or found online. The agent logs the source, contact, a summary, key stats, caveats, and best-use notes. A second ClickUp agent reviews the list when outlining article updates, so relevant statistics get surfaced automatically.
whatSurprisedMe: I receive a lot of press releases and studies that seem like they could be helpful one day, but I was never sure what to do with them to remember they existed. This keeps them all in one place and allows my agents to unearth them as needed.
whatWorked: You can direct the agent to check your email for the source material, or copy and paste it directly into the chat. The agent extracts structure from whatever you give it — press releases, PDFs, links — and files them in a consistent format with methodology details, key stats, caveats, and suggested editorial use.
nextTime: Make sure the agent can extract data from the file format you're sharing. Flag any conflicts of interest and double-check that the main stats are accurate — though this can also happen later in the fact-checking stage.

title: Giving the AI a named persona makes pitch prep sharper and more honest
whatTried: Created a specific AI persona — a manager named Michael — to review analysis and surface missing perspectives before client or pitch meetings.
whatSurprisedMe: The persona framing made the AI's feedback more critical and useful than asking generically. It role-played as a skeptical reviewer rather than a yes-machine.
whatWorked: Asking the persona to act as a quality assurance reviewer or critical developer. The named-character framing shifted the output from supportive to genuinely evaluative.
